clue.text: Pastry from Greek island area

parts.note: Samos is an island in the eastern Aegean

explanation.surface: A tourist buys a pastry somewhere on a Greek island.
explanation.definitionFit: A fried triangular pastry case filled with spiced vegetables or meat, from South Asian cooking.

clue.text: Temporary measures to prevent cavities

parts.note: to stop something is to prevent it
gaps are holes or cavities

explanation.surface: A dentist's makeshift fillings that stop cavities forming.
explanation.definitionFit: Makeshift arrangements that fill in for something until a permanent fix arrives.

clue.text: Month in which model gets just a bit staid and plumpish

indicators.note: in which says the model goes inside the month

parts.note: Mar is the abbreviation for March
the Model T was Ford's famous car, so T can stand for model
just means only

explanation.surface: In one month a model becomes a little staid and plump.
explanation.walkthrough: MAY is the tempting month, but it cannot hold the pieces; MAR (March) takes T inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Describes a woman of dignified middle-aged bearing and a fuller figure, like a hospital's senior nurse.

clue.text: Silly moo x 3? Not right now

indicators.note: silly means foolish or muddled, so the letters are shuffled

parts.note: x 3 is read out as three times

explanation.surface: Calling someone a silly moo three times over, and putting off a reply.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'x 3' as the words THREE TIMES; with MOO they rearrange to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A polite way of postponing: at a later occasion, not at present.

clue.text: Women's groups note song about climber

parts.note: WI is the Women's Institute, so several of them are WIS
te is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

indicators.note: about here means turned around, so the word for the song is read backwards

parts.note: an air is a song or tune

explanation.surface: Women's Institute branches note down a song about some climbing plant.
explanation.walkthrough: The Women's Institute is a British countrywomen's organisation with local branches. 'about' here signals a turnaround, not a container.
explanation.definitionFit: Wisteria is a woody vine with hanging lilac flowers, a classic example of a climbing plant.

clue.text: Putting a bun in the oven, mischief-maker and sailor eat last of the egg and bacon

definitions.text: Putting a bun in the oven

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous little creature

indicators.note: eat suggests taking food inside, so the sailor surrounds the picked letters

parts.note: a rating is a non-commissioned sailor

indicators.note: last of picks the final letter of each of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A cheeky line about a scamp and a sailor eating a fry-up of egg and bacon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eat' is the container signal: the sailor swallows the final letters. 'Putting a bun in the oven' is British slang for getting pregnant.
explanation.definitionFit: To have a bun in the oven is to be pregnant, so causing that state means making a woman pregnant.

clue.text: Setter uses this repeatedly

parts.note: the word setter contains TT

explanation.surface: The setter keeps using this, again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: abbreviate the answer to T after T and you get the TT in the middle of 'Setter'. The puzzle's theme is time.
explanation.definitionFit: Over and over again, on many occasions; a stock phrase meaning frequently.

clue.text: Bust bouncing about in red underwear, initially

indicators.note: bouncing about suggests things jumping around, so the letters are jumbled
initially picks out the opening letter of underwear

explanation.surface: A bust bouncing around in red lingerie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' gives the U of 'underwear', which joins IN RED before 'bouncing about' rearranges them. 'Bust' looks like a body part but is the slang adjective for broken.
explanation.definitionFit: Bust here is slang for broken or bankrupt, synonymous with wrecked and destroyed.

clue.text: Theatre cat in season? Only half a month

indicators.note: in places the cat inside the half-season
only half says just the first half of the season word is used

parts.note: autumn is one of the four seasons
Gus the Theatre Cat is one of T. S. Eliot's Practical Cats, also in the musical Cats

explanation.surface: A theatre cat in season, but only for half a month.
explanation.walkthrough: The theatre cat is Gus from T. S. Eliot's cat poems, which became the musical Cats.
explanation.definitionFit: The eighth month of the calendar, named after the Roman emperor Augustus.

clue.text: Prompt outburst of emotion, not love

indicators.note: an outburst scatters things wildly, so the letters of emotion are thrown into a new order
not tells us one piece is absent from the letters being rearranged

parts.note: love is nil in tennis scoring, written as the letter O

explanation.surface: A timely outburst of emotion that has no love in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not love' takes an O out of EMOTION, leaving EMTION; 'outburst of' rearranges those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Being prompt means arriving punctually, at the appointed hour rather than late.

clue.text: Make notes about girl, first of many sending junk mail

indicators.note: about means going around, so the singing word surrounds the rest

parts.note: to sing is to make musical notes with the voice
Pam is a girl's name

indicators.note: first of picks out the opening letter of the next word

explanation.surface: Someone jots notes about a girl, the first of many people sending out junk mail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make notes' looks like writing things down, but here it means singing.
explanation.definitionFit: Spam is unsolicited bulk email, so flooding inboxes with it is this activity.

clue.text: Occult practitioner molesting our doctors

indicators.note: doctors as a verb means tampers with or falsifies, so the letters are altered

explanation.surface: A sinister headline about a practitioner of the occult molesting our doctors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doctors' looks like a noun but is a verb meaning tampers with, which rearranges MOLESTING OUR.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who claims numbers have mystic significance in people's lives, a form of divination.

clue.text: Former monarch, half German?

parts.note: the first half of the word German is GER, which is G (the usual abbreviation for ...) followed by ER, Elizabeth Regina, the royal cipher of Elizabeth I

explanation.surface: A quiz question: was some former monarch half German?
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: abbreviate the answer, G for 'good' and ER (Elizabeth Regina) for the queen, and you get GER, half of 'German'. The surface tempts you toward Hanoverian kings.
explanation.definitionFit: This was the affectionate popular name for Elizabeth I, England's Tudor queen who reigned from 1558 to 1603.

Somehow paint ankle and feet without using an artist's spatula

indicators.note: somehow suggests the letters get put together in some unspecified way, so they are rearranged
without using tells us some letters of the pool are left out

explanation.surface: Paint your ankle and feet somehow, but without using an artist's spatula.
explanation.walkthrough: 'an' looks like part of the definition, but 'without using an' removes one A and one N from the pooled letters before the rearrangement.

clue.text: Bound to live with Amanda?

parts.note: to be is to exist, or live
Amanda Holden is a British actress and TV presenter, a judge on Britain's Got Talent

explanation.surface: Is someone destined to live with a woman called Amanda?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that Amanda is a definition by example: the solver needs her surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Being indebted or obliged to someone, as in bound by a debt of gratitude.

clue.text: Ship carrying right flag — a narrow one

indicators.note: carrying means holding something inside, so the ship surrounds the letter

parts.note: a steamer is a steamship

explanation.surface: A ship carrying the right flag, a long narrow one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carrying' puts R inside STEAMER.
explanation.definitionFit: A long thin pennant or ribbon flown from a mast, like a narrow banner.

clue.text: He let wobble go wobbly ahead of time? That's not fair!

indicators.note: ahead of places the rearranged letters before the next piece
letters that go wobbly lose their order and settle into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone let a jelly wobble and it went wobbly too soon, which hardly seems fair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go wobbly' rearranges HELETWOBBLE; 'ahead of' puts that before T.
explanation.definitionFit: From boxing, where a punch below the waistline breaks the rules; hence any unfair or underhand remark or act.

clue.text: After queueing first starts, there's always a serious complaint

indicators.note: starts picks the opening letters of the two words before it

parts.note: ever means always, as in ever hopeful

explanation.surface: After queueing, the first to start always has a serious complaint to make.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts' takes Q and F from 'queueing' and 'first'; 'complaint' is used in its medical sense, an illness.
explanation.definitionFit: A bacterial infection caught from farm animals, causing high temperatures; a serious illness or ailment.

clue.text: Cook too much food, revoltingly somewhat on the turn

indicators.note: on the turn says the hidden letters are read backwards
somewhat says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Overcooked food tastes revolting and is going off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the turn' sounds like food going sour, but it turns the hidden letters around.
explanation.definitionFit: To overcook something is to leave it on the heat past the right point.

clue.text: Evelyn regularly has enough for ten LPs

parts.note: the alternate letters of Evelyn are V, L, N

explanation.surface: Evelyn regularly saves up to buy a stack of ten long-playing records.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: shorten the answer to V, L, N and you get every other letter of 'Evelyn'. In the definition LP is 50p, L being Roman fifty and P pence, so ten of them make five pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Ten fifty-pence pieces add up to five pounds sterling, the value of this British banknote.

Girl in a state (in Havana)

definitions.meaning: a US state on the Atlantic coast, abbreviated VA

explanation.surface: A girl in some state while visiting Havana.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket is a further hint: VA, the state's abbreviation, sits inside 'Havana'. Havana also suggests cigars, and the state is famed for its tobacco.

clue.text: Missing male member of French man, originally a politician

parts.note: a member is a limb; with M (male) missing from that word, three letters remain
de is French for of

indicators.note: originally points to the opening letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A Frenchman who has lost his male member, originally a politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Missing male member' is a limb without its M, the abbreviation for male. A Lib Dem is a member of Britain's Liberal Democrat party.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for Liberal Democrat, the centrist UK party, so a person belonging to it is a politician.

clue.text: Romeo going off with Juliet at last, having discontented time in cramped accommodation?

indicators.note: going off suggests the name breaking down into disorder, so its letters are rearranged
at last picks the final letter of the name before it
discontented means with its contents emptied, leaving only the outside letters

explanation.surface: Romeo leaves with Juliet, unhappy after an uncomfortable time in tiny lodgings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going off' rearranges ROMEO to ROOME; 'at last' gives T from Juliet; 'discontented' empties TIME to TE.
explanation.definitionFit: A small private sleeping compartment on an American railway car, so a tight space to stay in.

clue.text: Cheesemaker's backing? It's worth two 23 24 25s

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the word is read in reverse

parts.note: rennet is the enzyme used to curdle milk in cheesemaking

explanation.surface: What backs the cheesemaker's business is worth a couple of banknotes.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition refers to the linked answer at 23, the five-pound note; two of them make this ten-pound note.
explanation.definitionFit: A British ten-pound note, worth exactly twice the value of the fiver at the cross-reference.
